{{Short description|Topological space}}
In [[topology]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''loop space''' Ω''X'' of a [[Pointed space|pointed]] [[topological space]] ''X'' is the space of (based) loops in ''X'', i.e. [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]] pointed maps from the pointed [[circle]] ''S''<sup>1</sup> to ''X'', equipped with the [[compact-open topology]]. Two loops can be multiplied by [[path (topology)#Path composition|concatenation]]. With this operation, the loop space is an [[A-infinity operad|''A''<sub>∞</sub>-space]]. That is, the multiplication is [[Homotopy|homotopy-coherently]] [[associative property|associative]].

The [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[path component]]s of Ω''X'', i.e. the set of based-homotopy [[equivalence class]]es of based loops in ''X'', is a [[Group (mathematics)|group]], the [[fundamental group]] ''&pi;''<sub>1</sub>(''X'').

The '''iterated loop spaces''' of ''X'' are formed by applying Ω a number of times.

There is an analogous construction for topological spaces without basepoint. The '''free loop space''' of a topological space ''X'' is the space of maps from the circle ''S''<sup>1</sup> to ''X'' with the compact-open topology. The free loop space of ''X'' is often denoted by <math>\mathcal{L}X</math>. 
 
As a [[functor]], the free loop space construction is [[right adjoint]] to [[cartesian product]] with the circle, while the loop space construction is right adjoint to the [[reduced suspension]]. This adjunction accounts for much of the importance of loop spaces in [[stable homotopy theory]]. (A related phenomenon in [[computer science]] is [[currying]], where the cartesian product is adjoint to the [[hom functor]].) Informally this is referred to as [[Eckmann–Hilton duality]].

== Eckmann–Hilton duality ==
The loop space is dual to the [[Suspension (topology)|suspension]] of the same space; this duality is sometimes called [[Eckmann–Hilton duality]]. The basic observation is that
:<math>[\Sigma Z,X] \approxeq [Z, \Omega X]</math>
where <math>[A,B]</math> is the set of homotopy classes of maps <math>A \rightarrow B</math>,
and <math>\Sigma A</math> is the suspension of A, and <math>\approxeq</math> denotes the [[Natural transformation|natural]] [[homeomorphism]].  This homeomorphism is essentially that of [[currying]], modulo the quotients needed to convert the products to reduced products.

In general, <math>[A, B]</math> does not have a group structure for arbitrary spaces <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>. However, it can be shown that <math>[\Sigma Z,X]</math> and <math>[Z, \Omega X]</math> do have natural group structures when <math>Z</math> and <math>X</math> are [[Pointed space|pointed]], and the aforementioned isomorphism is of those groups.<ref name="may">{{citation |last= May |first=J. P. |authorlink=J. Peter May|title=A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology |year=1999 |publisher=U. Chicago Press, Chicago |url=http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/CONCISE/ConciseRevised.pdf |accessdate=2016-08-27}} ''(See chapter 8, section 2)''</ref>  Thus, setting <math>Z = S^{k-1}</math> (the <math>k-1</math> sphere) gives the relationship

:<math>\pi_k(X) \approxeq \pi_{k-1}(\Omega X)</math>.

This follows since the [[homotopy group]] is defined as <math>\pi_k(X)=[S^k,X]</math> and the spheres can be obtained via suspensions of each-other, i.e. <math>S^k=\Sigma S^{k-1}</math>.<ref>[http://topospaces.subwiki.org/wiki/Loop_space_of_a_based_topological_space Topospaces wiki – Loop space of a based topological space]</ref>
